q: What is Figure A, a structural element typically used to support roof or wall cladding in steel buildings?
n: Figure A is a Z purlin, a cold-formed section supporting roof or wall cladding in steel buildings. It laps for continuity. Source: AISI S100; Ching.

q: What is Figure B, a horizontal structural element used to support roofing and cladding systems in industrial or agricultural buildings?
n: Figure B is a C purlin (channel), a cold-formed member supporting roofing and cladding. Source: AISI S100; Ching.

q: What is Figure C, a structural element used to enhance support and reduce deflection in roof systems?
n: Figure C is a hat-section (top-hat) purlin, used as a batten or purlin to support cladding and reduce deflection. Source: Manufacturer data (light-gauge steel); Ching.

q: What is Figure D, a tension member used to prevent sagging and resist compressive forces in large roof structures?
n: Figure D is a sag rod, a tension rod between purlins that prevents sagging about their weak axis. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual; Ching.

q: What is Figure E, a device commonly used to adjust tension in cables or rods in structural applications?
n: Figure E is a turnbuckle, used to adjust tension in rods or cables. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is Figure A, a truss with diagonal members in compression and vertical members in tension, commonly used in residential construction?
n: A Howe truss has diagonals in compression and verticals in tension, the classic timber truss. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; Schodek, Structures.

q: What is Figure B, a truss with diagonal members in tension and vertical members in compression, typically used in long-span roofing systems?
n: A Pratt truss has diagonals in tension and verticals in compression, efficient for steel and long spans. Source: Schodek, Structures.

q: What is Figure C, a truss with a triangular design commonly used in residential roofing for steep roof structures?
n: A Fink truss has a W-shaped web inside a triangular profile and is common for steep residential roofs. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is Figure D, a truss designed to create vaulted ceilings, often used in churches and large halls?
n: A scissor truss has crossing bottom chords that create a vaulted ceiling, used in churches and halls. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is Figure E, a simple roof truss commonly used in residential buildings to support lean-to roofs?
n: Figure E is a simple rafter truss, sloping rafters with a tie, used for lean-to and simple residential roofs. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is Figure A, the horizontal or sloped member at the top of a truss that primarily carries compression forces?
n: Item A is the top chord, the upper (sloped) member of a truss, which mainly carries compression. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; Schodek, Structures.

q: What is Figure B, a metal plate used to connect and reinforce the joints of a truss by holding the members together?
n: Item B is a truss plate (gusset or nail plate) that connects members at a joint. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; TPI 1.

q: What is Figure C, a diagonal or vertical member that connects the top and bottom chords in a truss, typically under tension or compression?
n: Item C is a web member, a diagonal or vertical linking the chords and carrying tension or compression. Source: Schodek, Structures.

q: What is Figure D, the horizontal or sloped member at the bottom of a truss that typically carries tension forces?
n: Item D is the bottom chord, which typically carries tension. The bottom chord ties the truss ends together and resists the outward thrust of the sloping top chords. Source: Schodek, Structures.

q: What is Figure E, the portion of a truss that extends beyond the main support, usually to cover an eaves or overhang area?
n: Item E is the overhang, the part of the truss extending past the support to form the eaves. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Identify Figure A that is the point where the bottom chord and the top chord of a truss meet, typically located at the end support.
n: Item A is the heel, where top and bottom chords meet at the end support. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; TPI terminology.

q: Identify Figure B that is the horizontal extension of the top chord beyond the support, often used for eaves or shading.
n: Item B is the overhang, the top chord's extension beyond the support for eaves or shading. Source: TPI terminology; Ching.

q: Identify Figure C that is a connection where two segments of a truss member are joined together to form a longer piece.
n: Item C is a splice, where two segments of a truss member are joined into a longer piece. Source: TPI terminology.

q: Identify Figure D that is an internal diagonal or vertical member of a truss that transfers loads between the chords.
n: Item D is a web member, an internal diagonal or vertical that transfers load between the chords. Source: Schodek, Structures.

q: Identify Figure E that is a horizontal support member installed between trusses to prevent buckling of the web members.
n: Item E is a continuous lateral brace, running between trusses to keep web members from buckling. Source: SBCA/TPI BCSI (Building Component Safety Information).

q: What do you call a rod placed between purlins to serve as bridging and prevent misalignment?
n: A bridging rod placed between purlins keeps them aligned and braces their weak axis. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; AISC.

q: What is the primary purpose of sag rods?
n: Sag rods support purlins that would otherwise sag about their weak axis. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual; Ching.

q: What do sag rods do in roof framing?
o: Keep purlins from sagging or bending sideways
n: Sag rods keep purlins from sagging or bending sideways along the roof slope (weak-axis bracing). Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual.

q: Z purlins on a truss sloped 20° tend to sag under dead and live load. Which member gives them support along their weak axis?
n: On a sloped roof, part of the load acts along the slope on the purlin's weak axis. Sag rods give that support. Source: AISI S100; AISC.

q: What usually supports purlins?
n: Purlins span between and are supported by trusses (or rafters). Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which of the following is NOT a part of a roof truss?
n: A roof truss is made of chords and webs joined by gusset plates. A fastener is hardware, not a truss part. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which of the following is NOT typically required in a roof system?
n: Sag rods, truss rods and queen posts are roof-system members. Camber is a built-in curvature, not a required component. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Why does a truss have a bottom chord?
o: A truss can't span without it
To limit sag and carry tension
n: The bottom chord ties the truss ends together, carrying tension and limiting sag and spread. Source: Schodek, Structures.

q: What connects truss members at their joints?
n: Gusset plates connect truss members at their joints. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is the standard size of purlins?
n: Wood purlins are commonly 2 × 3 in. in Philippine residential roofs. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (roof framing).

q: What section is typical for roof purlins?
n: Cold-formed C-channel purlins are typical for roofs. Source: AISI S100; Philippine steel suppliers' data.

q: What is the standard spacing of purlins for corrugated roofing?
n: For corrugated GI sheets, purlins are commonly spaced about 600 mm on centre. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (roofing); manufacturer data.

q: What purlin section is most used locally?
n: Light-gauge C-purlins are the most used purlin section locally. Source: Philippine steel suppliers' data; Fajardo.

q: What is the typical distance between roof purlins?
n: Roof purlins are typically spaced about 0.60 m apart for corrugated sheets. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: Which one is a cantilever wall?
n: Figure B is a cantilever wall: a reinforced stem fixed to a base slab (toe and heel). Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering; NSCP 2015 Sec. 304.
